title: Architecture Decision Record (ADR) 001
text:
Date: October 2026


The Arclight-Epi project requires a natural language processing pipeline capable of extracting structured triage line-lists from unstructured epidemiological field data. This tool is designed for deployment in public health settings, which introduces strict operational constraints. Relying on commercial, cloud-based Large Language Model (LLM) APIs introduces unacceptable risks regarding Protected Health Information (PHI) governance, data sovereignty, and variable per-token inference costs. Furthermore, field epidemiologists often operate in environments with limited or no internet connectivity, rendering cloud-dependent architectures unreliable.



We will implement a local-first, edge-deployed architecture utilizing a sub-3B parameter Small Language Model (SLM) in quantized GGUF format. The model will execute entirely offline on commodity hardware to perform zero-shot or few-shot structured data extraction.




Data Privacy & Security By Design: Executing the model locally ensures that zero PHI leaves the host machine. This bypasses the need for complex Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) with external cloud providers and inherently complies with HIPAA and local data sovereignty laws.
Operational Resilience: A fully offline architecture guarantees 100% uptime for field operatives in remote or undeveloped settings, removing network latency and connectivity as points of failure.
Cost Containment: By avoiding commercial API calls, the enterprise avoids runaway inference costs. The compute burden is shifted to existing edge hardware (e.g., standard laptops), reducing ongoing operational expenditures to zero.
Right-Sizing Compute: Triage data extraction is a bounded, specific task. Deploying a massive frontier model (e.g., 70B+ parameters) is architecturally bloated for this use case. A 1.5B to 3B parameter model provides sufficient linguistic capability while fitting comfortably within the memory constraints of a standard CPU/RAM footprint.





Trade-off: Reduced Generalized Reasoning: Small models lack the broad reasoning capabilities of frontier models.

Mitigation: We will utilize strict constrained decoding (forcing the model to output specific JSON/CSV schemas) and specialized prompt engineering to narrow the model’s focus strictly to the extraction task.

Trade-off: Evaluation Complexity: Ensuring clinical accuracy without a massive parameter count requires rigorous validation.

Mitigation: We will develop a comprehensive, offline evaluation harness prior to deployment to benchmark extraction accuracy, measure missingness diagnostics, and quantify hallucination rates.

title: 01 - Development Plan
text:
Note



Arclight follows principles of MVP development and separation of concerns. The main Arclight model will be the initial release, developed, optimized, and made available in a standalone ONNX format. A quantized version will then be developed as an integrated Shiny app packaged in a deployable Docket container. The fully integrated Flutter application will be the final release, initially targeting Android, Windows, and Linux systems.

title: 01 - Development Plan
text:
Phase 1: Model Development & Optimization
Train, validate, and optimize machine learning models before exporting for on-device execution, publishing source code under an open-source license.

Tasks:

Baseline Model Development: Develop, train, and validate initial model
Optimization & Quantization: Apply post-training quantization and model compression techniques to minimize memory footprint and optimize execution speed for target end-user devices.
ONNX Export: Export tuned models into the industry standard ONNX format required for widespread mobile and desktop release.
Open-Source Licensing: Host model source code and assets on GitHub under the GNU General Public License v3.0 (GPL v3.0).

title: 01 - Development Plan
section: Phase 2: UI/UX Proof of Concept (Shiny & Docker)
text:
Phase 2: UI/UX Proof of Concept (Shiny & Docker)
Prototype the user interface and validate operational workflows quickly through a web-based Proof of Concept (POC).

Tasks:

Shiny Prototype: Build a functional Shiny interface to mock up layouts, data ingestion workflows, and visualization formats required for different end-use cases.
Workflow Validation: Test end-to-end data processing, user interaction flows, and structured decision-support outputs within the Shiny workspace.
Docker Containerization: Package the Shiny application into a Docker container for isolated testing, streamlined sharing, and collecting feedback from epidemiologists and stakeholders.

title: 01 - Development Plan
text:
Phase 3: Flutter Application Development & Integration
Construct the production cross-platform native application framework and integrate local machine learning models into the Dart pipeline.

Tasks:

App Scaffolding & Front-End: Develop responsive front-end UI components in Flutter supporting Android, Linux, and Windows targeting cross-platform consistency.
Dart Data Pipeline: Implement data import, sanitization, and preprocessing functions in Dart to prepare user inputs for model consumption.
On-Device Model Integration: Integrate exported .onnx models into the Flutter application for privacy-preserving, local execution.
Secure Local Storage: Implement encrypted local databases (e.g., SQLite or Hive) with local encrypted backups to external storage media like USB drives.

title: 01 - Development Plan
text:
Phase 4: Integration Testing & Multi-Platform Deployment
Conduct rigorous system-wide testing and publish production application builds across supported platforms and repositories.

Tasks:

Integration Testing: Perform comprehensive integration testing across Android, iOS, and Windows, verifying on-device model accuracy, UI responsiveness, PHI censoring algorithms during PDF/CSV exports, and database security.
App Store & Open-Source Distribution: Publish finalized production binaries to app stores (Google Play Store, Apple App Store, Microsoft Store) and release full source code and build distributions on GitHub.

title: Hi, I’m Matt Scruggs, MPH, MSDA
text:
I am a data science leader specializing in the intersection of machine learning and infectious disease. By combining a Master of Public Health and Epidemiology with a Master of Science in Data Analytics, I build targeted artificial intelligence systems designed for the realities of field medicine.
Currently, I am developing Arclight-FEBE, a proof-of-concept small language model engineered for the epidemiology domain. It serves as the foundation for the broader Arclight reference architecture: a framework for deploying local, edge-capable language models that prioritize data privacy, offline functionality, and operational resilience in restricted environments.

title: Hi, I’m Matt Scruggs, MPH, MSDA
text:
The Arclight Thesis
The future of AI belongs to local, private, offline models running on edge devices which are capable of accomplishing 95% of real-world use cases.

Local AI Follows the Arc of History
We’ve seen this path before, from the earliest days of digital devices. Computer mainframes were initially tested and experimented with in academic and commercial labs. Computation then spread to enterprise and government end users via centralized mainframes leased or sold to enterprises, with proprietary restrictions. Continued developments and improvements led to personal computers, and, years later, smartphones, following consumer demand for convenience, personalization, privacy, and sovereignty. As devices became more accessible and personal, demand exploded, and led to follow-on technologies like the internet, social media, and an entirely new on-demand digitally enabled economic sector, all of which would be impossible without the move from mainframe to smartphone.


AI Needs a Sustainable Path Forward
Cutting-edge foundation models running on massive data centers are financially and ecologically unsustainable, and unnecessary for 95% of real-world end uses. Custom-built local AI implementations, tuned for specific end uses, and running on edge devices, are environmentally friendly, require no incremental inference costs, isolate user data by design, and remove vulnerabilities to token cost inflation or changes to terms and services agreements. This design philosophy could increase access and adoption globally, with countless follow-on benefits similar to those seen with the democratization of computation through smartphone proliferation.

Arclight is a reference architecture designed to make this dream possible.

title: About Matt Scruggs
text:
Hi, I’m Matt Scruggs. I’m a data science professional and epidemiologist passionate about solving humanity’s toughest problems with our best technology.
As a data science leader and builder, I translate strategic vision into scalable machine learning and AI implementations across industries such as automotive, pharmaceuticals, insurance, and banking. My expertise lies in deploying high-impact applications from concept to production, empowering multi-disciplinary teams to deliver robust, scalable solutions.
Over more than a decade of technical leadership, I have built and scaled high-performing data science and analytics teams from the ground up within both greenfield and highly regulated environments. Operating as a player-coach who bridges executive roadmapping with direct architectural implementation, I focus on transforming ambiguous challenges into deployable intelligence systems that drive measurable business outcomes while maintaining rigorous governance.
My academic background bridges public health and advanced analytics. I hold a Master’s degree in Public Health with a post-graduate certification in Epidemiology, as well as a Master’s degree in Data Analytics with a post-graduate certification in Machine Learning, uniting a deep passion for using artificial intelligence to combat infectious disease.
Outside of my core professional responsibilities, I spearhead independent research in local-first edge AI architectures for field epidemiology. This includes developing Arclight-FEBE, an offline, sub-8B parameter small language model engineered from scratch in PyTorch to function as a deterministic semantic compiler for public health field operations in resource-constrained environments.

title: The Frontier Fallacy
text:
Flying the World’s Heaviest Airplane
When a health tech organization decides to implement artificial intelligence today, the default instinct is almost always to reach for the biggest cloud-hosted engine on the market. These massive, multi-billion and trillion-parameter frontier systems are engineering marvels, capable of composing sonnets, answering trivia, and simulating natural human banter. Yet when deployed into clinical environments, this broad capability introduces severe operational baggage. Healthcare workflows rarely demand an open-ended conversationalist; they require precise, repetitive execution across structured data tasks. Piped through external cloud APIs, these generalist giants saddle health systems with unpredictable monthly bills, noticeable seconds of network latency, and persistent regulatory anxiety over data exposure and HIPAA compliance. Paying for an ocean of world knowledge when you only need a pipeline to parse medical records is an expensive mismatch.


Surgery Needs Scalpels, Not Chainsaws
The path forward is not to abandon modern language processing, but to rethink its scale entirely. Rather than relying on massive cloud models designed to do everything passably well, engineering teams should turn toward small, specialized models featuring architectures under 3 billion parameters, and trained or tuned specifically on biomedical schemas and clinical terminology. Organizations do not need a model that knows 19th-century history to extract a patient’s symptom timeline or parse an unstructured lab intake form. By scoping the model’s linguistic focus strictly to the language of medicine and constraining its output to rigid formats like JSON, a compact engine running locally can easily out-execute a distant supercomputer. The path forward is to treat artificial intelligence like a purpose-built instrument rather than an unconstrained chatbot.
The business and operational returns of this architectural shift are immediate. Organizations that transition specialized tasks away from commercial cloud endpoints routinely see inferencing costs drop by more than 90%. Because small, specialized models are compact enough to run on dedicated, containerized internal hardware or local machines, per-token billing volatility is replaced with fixed, predictable compute expenses. Latency falls from seconds down to milliseconds, and structured output constraints virtually eliminate the formatting hallucinations common in chatty foundation models. Most importantly, sensitive protected health information never has to leave the local network, entirely eliminating the attack surface and compliance headaches of third-party cloud data transit.
Right-sizing your model architecture to match task complexity is an engineering and budgetary discipline, not a compromise. For AI systems deployed in healthcare settings,functional, reliable, and secure execution always wins.

title: Arclight-FEBE v1.0
text:
Local health departments operate on the front lines of disease surveillance and outbreak response, yet they routinely face severe resource constraints. Persistent underfunding and staffing shortages make deploying complex cloud infrastructure, managing heavy pipelines, or maintaining continuous subscription APIs practical impossibilities.
Furthermore, field epidemiologists work in harsh environments where connectivity is unreliable. Data collected during investigations is complex, highly contextual, and contains sensitive Protected Health Information (PHI). Standard consumer AI models carry severe data privacy risks and offer little defense against hallucinations, risking misallocated resources and public mistrust.

title: Arclight-FEBE v1.0
text:
Bridging the Gap: On-Device AI
Critical public health interventions rarely occur in climate-controlled offices; they unfold in rural clinics, border settlements, and post-disaster zones. Because modern tools rely heavily on the cloud, a dropped connection instantly freezes applications, forcing responders back to manual paper forms at the exact moment rapid data processing is vital.
To solve this, public health tech must deploy local-first, quantized machine learning. By utilizing small language models (<3B parameters) optimized for standard laptops and tablets, applications become fully self-sufficient. These specialized models extract symptoms, timelines, and risk factors from messy notes directly on-device without calling external servers.

title: Arclight-FEBE v1.0
section: The Arclight Solution: On-Device AI for Frontline Response
text:
The Arclight Solution: On-Device AI for Frontline Response
Designed explicitly for edge deployment, the Arclight architecture runs natively on handheld devices. By eliminating external network dependencies, it removes cloud setup overhead, API subscription costs, and data leakage risks. Despite a compact footprint, Arclight ingests unstructured field notes, images, and voice recordings, outputting tightly structured formats for dependable analytical use in any off-grid environment.

title: Arclight-FEBE v1.0
text:
Introducing Arclight-FEBE
The Arclight- Field Epidemiology By Epidemiologists (FEBE) project serves as an open-source proof of concept demonstrating Arclight in practice. FEBE provides an accessible framework for academic and research institutions worldwide to build, adapt, and deploy custom epidemiological tools directly into field hands.

title: Arclight-FEBE v1.0
text:
Zero-Trust AI
Running inference locally establishes a zero-trust privacy perimeter. Because sensitive patient details never leave the physical hard drive, organizations overcome major regulatory hurdles, avoid recurring server costs, and maintain complete data residency by default. Ultimately, sustainable AI for public health must treat internet connectivity as an unpredictable variable rather than a core requirement—ensuring field operations remain resilient against any crisis.

text: The Engineering Log

title: 02 - Architectural Design
text:
Arclight’s architecture is built on a modular, cross-platform framework that prioritizes on-device execution to ensure absolute privacy for Protected Health Information (PHI) and independence from cloud infrastructure. The methodology for integrating machine learning capabilities into the application is divided into model development and front-end integration.


Below is a visual representation of the lifecycle of an Arclight ML module, from development to on-device output:





---
config:
  theme: neo
  look: neo
  layout: dagre
---
flowchart TD
    subgraph Model Development
        Dev("Pre-Training")
        Fine("Retrieval Fine-Tuning")
        Eval("Model Evaluation")
    end
    GPL("Deploy under GPL 3.0 license")
    subgraph Shiny POC
        UI("UI Mockup")
        Opt("Model Quantization and Optimization")
        Int("Model Integration")
        Dock("Dockerize")
    end
    subgraph Flutter Module
        Pre("Data Import & Preprocessing in Dart")
        Loc("Local Model Execution")
        Out("Output Formatting & Display")
    end
    Dev --> Fine
    Fine --> Eval
    Eval --> GPL
    Eval --> UI
    UI --> Opt
    Opt --> Int
    Int --> Dock
    Dock --> GPL
    Dock --> Pre
    Pre --> Loc
    Loc --> Out
    Out --> GPL









The core encoder retrieval model is adapted and optimized for local, low-latency execution on device.

Domain Focus: End-to-end domain specific training to optimize retrieval across keywords and semantic layers.
Export & Quantization: Export the model and retrieval pipelines into the open ONNX format, applying quantization to optimize memory usage and performance across desktop and mobile devices.




Prior to the full mobile and desktop rollout, a containerized prototype is constructed using Shiny to validate workflows and user experience:

Rapid Prototyping: Build a web-based proof-of-concept to test local language model processing and visual outputs with stakeholders.
Containerization: Package the Shiny interface and quantized ONNX runtime inside a Docker container to ensure reproducible testing across different evaluation environments.
Workflow Validation: Gather user feedback on interactive reporting features—including dynamic maps, tables, and epidemic curves—to refine UI/UX specifications before native app development.




The core application is built using the Flutter framework, enabling a single codebase to deploy across Android, Windows, and Linux. For the local model integration, a standardized process is followed within the Dart codebase:

Front-End Design: Develop the responsive front-end user interface components in Flutter to capture inputs (text, audio, images).
Data Import & Preprocessing: Write robust data ingestion and preprocessing handlers in Dart to prepare inputs for model compatibility.
Model Execution: Invoke the quantized ONNX model locally using cross-platform ONNX Runtime bindings in Dart to run inferences strictly on-device.
Output Formatting: Capture the inference results, process and format them (generating charts, tables, maps, or textual decision support), and display them within the UI.

This workflow ensures on-device reasoning and privacy preservation across all target platforms.
